chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Wider Lens on Risk

lessons.title: The Illiquidity Premium: Getting Paid to Lock Your Money Away

children.text: Kavya, a 39-year-old radiologist in Ahmedabad, has two options for ₹1 crore. She can buy a Nifty 50 index fund today and sell it any working day she likes. Or she can commit to a private equity fund that will return her money over roughly ten years, on its own schedule. Nobody sensible picks the second option at the same expected return. So how much extra should she demand for giving up her exit, and will she actually receive it? That extra is the illiquidity premium, and it is the single best reason to own alternatives at all.

body.text: The illiquidity premium is a price, not a gift. You are selling your flexibility to the market. Get paid enough for it, only sell flexibility you truly do not need, and make sure fees do not take the payment before it reaches you.

children.text: What the Premium Pays You For

markDefs.definition: The extra expected return investors demand for holding an asset that cannot be sold quickly at a fair price, compared with a similar asset that can.

children.text: The
illiquidity premium
is the extra return, over a comparable liquid asset, that compensates you for three real costs:
Lost flexibility.
You cannot use the money for an emergency, a better opportunity or a rebalance.
Forced-sale risk.
If you do have to get out, you may have to accept a steep discount.
Timing uncertainty.
You do not control when cash comes back, so you cannot plan around it precisely.

body.caption: Compare like with like: private equity with listed equity, private credit with listed bonds

body.text: Keep the premium separate from other extra returns. A private credit fund's higher yield also includes a credit premium for lending to riskier borrowers, which Lesson 2 of Chapter 1 deducted as expected losses. The illiquidity premium is only the part you earn for being locked in.

children.text: How the Premium Actually Shows Up: The Entry Discount

markDefs.definition: A reduction valuers apply to the value of shares or stakes that cannot easily be sold, to reflect the cost and delay of finding a buyer.

children.text: Nobody sends you a separate cheque labelled "illiquidity premium." You earn it mainly by paying less on the way in. When Indian valuers value unlisted shares, they often apply a
discount for lack of marketability
. If you buy at that discount and later exit at full value, the discount turns into extra annual return.

body.label: Discount for lack of marketability
body.context: A common range in valuations of unlisted Indian shares. The right number depends on the company, the stake size and how likely an exit is.

body.caption: d = entry discount to fair value, n = years until you exit at fair value

children.text: Suppose you buy shares of a profitable unlisted company at a 25% discount to what similar listed companies trade at, and it lists four years later at full value. The discount alone adds (1 ÷ 0.75)^(1/4) − 1, or about 7.5% a year, on top of whatever the business itself grows. That is a large premium. It also depends entirely on the exit arriving, on time, at full value.

body.caption: The same 25% entry discount, spread over different holding periods
headers: Years until exit at fair value
Extra annual return from the discount

children.text: Read that table carefully. The longer the wait, the thinner the premium per year. An IPO delayed from four years to ten turns a fat 7.5% premium into less than 3%, before counting the extra years of risk.

body.title: Convert a discount into a premium
body.prompt: You buy unlisted shares at a 20% discount to fair value and exit at fair value after 3 years. How much extra annual return did the discount add? Answer in percent, to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 1 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 1.25. Then 1.25^(1/3) − 1 ≈ 0.077, or about 7.7% a year. If the exit slips to 6 years, the same discount is worth only about 3.8% a year.

children.text: How Much Premium Is Reasonable to Demand?

There is no official number, and research on how much illiquid assets have really earned after fees is mixed. But experienced investors tend to demand premiums in roughly these ranges, measured against the closest liquid comparison.

children.text: Three Ways the Premium Leaks Away
Fees swallow it.
A PE fund may target a 4-point premium over listed equity before fees. A 2% management fee plus GST, and a 20% share of profits, can take most of it.
Crowds compete it away.

When money floods into a hot private market, entry prices rise and the discount shrinks. In unlisted share booms, dealer prices can run above the price at which a company eventually lists, which means buyers paid a premium for illiquidity instead of receiving one.
You get forced out.
The premium is earned only by investors who hold to the end. Sell early at a discount and you pay the illiquidity cost instead of collecting the reward.
Is the Premium Worth It? Kavya's Numbers

Assume Kavya expects about 12% a year from the Nifty 50 index fund over a decade. The PE fund targets 16% gross. After fees, a realistic net figure might be closer to 13%. Here is what each rate does to ₹1 crore over ten years, before tax.

body.title: Growth of ₹1 crore at different annual returns (₹ crore, illustrative)
What the 1-point net premium buys and costs Kavya

columns.label: What she gains
points: About ₹29 lakh more after ten years (₹3.39 crore vs ₹3.11 crore), if the fund delivers 13% net
Exposure to companies not available on NSE or BSE
A reported value that moves less in the short term

columns.label: What she gives up
points: Any access to ₹1 crore for about a decade
The ability to rebalance or exit if the fund disappoints
Certainty: a below-median manager could easily return less than the index
Simplicity: capital calls, distributions and more complex tax reporting

children.text: A 1-point net premium for ten years of lock-in and heavy manager risk is thin. Many experienced allocators would want at least 3 points net before committing. That does not make the fund a bad idea. It gives Kavya a clear bar to judge it against.
Only Sell Flexibility You Do Not Need

markDefs.definition: The share of your portfolio you can afford to lock away for years without ever needing it, after providing for emergencies and known future expenses.

children.text: The investors best placed to earn the premium are those with long horizons and predictable cash needs: family offices, endowments, and individuals who have already covered every rupee they might need in the next several years. Think of it as a
liquidity budget
: only money that falls in the last bucket should ever go into locked-up assets.

body.title: Who should harvest the premium?
body.question: Which investor is best placed to earn an illiquidity premium from a 10-year private equity fund?
options: A 30-year-old saving for a flat down payment in 3 years
A 58-year-old retiring in 2 years with no pension, whose savings must fund living expenses
A 45-year-old business owner with ₹12 crore, stable income, and all expenses for the next 7 years already covered
A 35-year-old whose only savings are ₹20 lakh in an emergency fund
body.explanation: Earning the premium requires money you will not need for the whole lock-in. The business owner has a large portfolio, steady income and known needs already provided for. Every other investor has a near-term need that a 10-year lock-in would collide with.

body.title: Name the discount
body.textWithBlank: The discount valuers apply to unlisted shares because they cannot easily be sold is called the discount for lack of ___.
body.explanation: The discount for lack of marketability (DLOM) is the valuation-side mirror of the illiquidity premium. Buy at that discount, exit at full value, and the discount becomes your extra return.

body.title: Mr Siddiqui's venture fund pitch
body.scenario: Mr Siddiqui, 56, lives in Lucknow and plans to retire in four years. He has ₹2 crore in savings and no pension. His wealth manager recommends putting ₹1 crore into a 10-year venture capital fund, saying: "VC gives you a 5% illiquidity premium over the stock market. You are being paid to be patient."
body.prompt: Explain what is wrong with this recommendation using the ideas from this lesson.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The lock-in collides with his needs. He retires in four years with no pension, so part of this money is likely to be needed well before year ten. Only money outside his liquidity budget should be locked away, and half of his total savings is far too much.
2. The premium is a target, not a promise. A 5% premium is roughly what investors demand from VC. It is not what every fund delivers, and after fees and carry the net premium can be much smaller.
3. Manager dispersion is extreme in VC. A below-median fund can return less than a Nifty index fund, or even lose money.
4. If he is forced to exit early, he pays the illiquidity cost instead of earning the premium, assuming he can find a buyer for his stake at all.
5. Concentration: ₹1 crore is 50% of his wealth in one illiquid, high-risk fund.

A more sensible approach: build his retirement income and near-term needs from liquid, lower-risk assets first. If any alternative allocation makes sense at all, it should be a small slice of money he will never need.

points: The illiquidity premium is the extra expected return you demand for giving up the ability to sell quickly at a fair price.
It pays you for lost flexibility, forced-sale risk and uncertain timing, measured against the closest liquid comparison.
You earn it mainly through a lower entry price. A 25% discount adds about 7.5% a year over four years, but under 3% a year over ten.
Fees, crowded markets and early exits can shrink the premium to nothing, or turn it negative.
A thin net premium, like 1 point for a 10-year lock-in, may not justify the loss of flexibility and the manager risk.
Only lock away money that sits outside your liquidity budget, after emergencies and known future needs are covered.
